analysis.one_liner: Imposes a $1,000 tax on every electric vehicle sale, plus $550 on heavy battery modules, to fund highways.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee since February 2025 with no action beyond its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a new federal excise tax of $1,000 on the sale of every electric vehicle and $550 on any battery module weighing more than 1,000 pounds, starting with sales after December 31, 2025. Gas-electric hybrids would be exempt. All the money collected would go to the Highway Trust Fund, the pot of gas-tax money that pays for roads. The argument behind it is that electric vehicle owners don't buy gasoline, so they don't pay the gas taxes that fund the roads they drive on; the bill makes them pay into road funding at the point of purchase instead.
analysis.who_benefits: The Highway Trust Fund and road programs gain a new revenue stream. Indirectly, oil and gas companies and makers of conventional hybrids gain, because a $1,000-plus penalty makes battery-powered cars more expensive relative to the alternatives.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Road funding, oil companies, hybrid makers

how_it_helps.text: The bill routes every dollar of the new excise taxes to the Highway Trust Fund, which pays for surface transportation programs and is currently funded mainly by gasoline taxes that electric vehicle owners never pay.

The tax applies at sale: $1,000 per electric vehicle and an additional $550 for each battery module weighing over 1,000 pounds, so owners of large electric trucks with heavy batteries would pay the most.
Hybrid vehicles are explicitly exempt, so drivers who still buy some gasoline keep paying the gas tax and would not owe the new charge.

analysis.who_pays: Buyers of electric vehicles pay the tax, rolled into the sticker price. Electric vehicle manufacturers and battery makers bear reduced demand, with the heaviest hit being makers of large-battery trucks that would owe both the vehicle tax and the battery-module tax.

drawbacks.text: A one-time $1,000 tax at purchase is far larger than what a typical driver owes in gas taxes in any single year, so the charge is much heavier than a true per-mile user fee would be, and it falls entirely on buyers of one technology.

Buyers of large electric pickups and SUVs can be taxed twice under the bill, once on the vehicle and again on each battery module over 1,000 pounds, while big fuel-burning trucks that wear the roads the most pay no new charge.
By raising the price of electric vehicles, the bill slows the shift away from gasoline, which works against air-quality and fuel-cost savings that come with electrification.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a legitimate fairness question here: electric vehicle drivers use public roads without contributing the gas taxes that maintain them. But this bill answers it with the bluntest possible tool, a large one-time sales tax that overshoots what any individual driver would owe in fuel taxes and doubles down on the heaviest electric vehicles. A per-mile charge or a fuel-equivalent rate would match costs to use far more closely. The net effect for most ordinary buyers is a $1,000-plus price increase on the cars, with road funding as the offsetting benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in February 2025 and has had no hearings, markup, or vote since.

narrative.text: Senator Deb Fischer introduced the Fair SHARE Act of 2025 in the Senate on February 12, 2025, joined by Senators Pete Ricketts and Cynthia Lummis.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, and the public action record shows no further steps since that referral.

The Congressional Research Service summary describes the bill as imposing a $1,000 excise tax on electric vehicle sales and a $550 tax on battery modules over 1,000 pounds, with collections transferred to the Highway Trust Fund.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody yet, because nothing has happened; if the bill stays buried, electric vehicle buyers and makers are better off, while the oil and gas industry keeps the status quo advantage over plug-in cars.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet; EV buyers avoid the tax for now

for.name: Sen. Deb Fischer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and cosponsors are Republicans; no Democrat has signed on and no opponent appears in the record because the bill has never moved.

industries.note: A $1,000 charge on every sale, plus $550 on heavy battery modules, would raise prices and cut demand for their cars. Their interest in blocking the bill lines up with buyers who would pay the tax.
By making gasoline-free cars more expensive, the tax slows the shift away from gasoline, protecting demand for the fuel. The industry's gain comes at the price electric vehicle buyers pay.
Hybrids are explicitly exempt from the tax, giving plug-in hybrids and gas cars a $1,000 price advantage over battery-electric models at the showroom.

The Highway Trust Fund, which is chronically short of revenue, would receive a dedicated new stream from the tax. Better-funded road repair is a genuine public benefit, though paid for by a narrow group of buyers.
The $550 charge on battery modules over 1,000 pounds falls on the makers and importers of the large battery packs used in electric trucks and long-range cars, pushing their costs into vehicle prices.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has had no movement in the Senate Finance Committee since its February 2025 referral, has only three Republican backers, and no Democratic cosponsor. Tax bills of this kind rarely reach the floor without committee action and broader support, so the realistic path is that it stalls in committee for the rest of this Congress.
